summary: Extends MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute (RFC 8029) so they can discover and exercise specific paths over Layer 2 ECMP across Link Aggregation Group interfaces. It also defines a way to learn the capabilities of a Label Switching Router. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When several physical links are bundled into one logical link, a ping is normally balanced across them at random. This document lets the tester ask for each member link in turn, so that a link which has quietly stopped working can be found.

subtitle: Teaching MPLS ping and traceroute to test every member link of a bundled link, not just the one a test packet happens to pick.

tldr.problem: When a label-switched path crosses a bundle of links, ping and traceroute cannot tell which member link a packet used, so a member link that has stopped forwarding labels goes unnoticed.
tldr.mechanism: The extensions add a capability TLV and a LAG description flag, so that a router can list the member links of a bundle and the test packets can be steered at each one in turn.
tldr.outcome: Every member link of a bundle can be tested, and the failure of one of them can be pinpointed. RFC 8611 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 9041.

today: RFC 8611 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019. It updates RFC 8029, and it was later updated by RFC 9041, which changed the registry it uses. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Bundled Links
sections.content:
The MPLS Label Switched Path Ping and Traceroute mechanisms of RFC 8029 are tools for diagnosing all the available Layer 3 paths of a label-switched path, including coverage of Layer 3 equal-cost multipath. In many MPLS networks, Link Aggregation Groups as defined in IEEE 802.1AX provide Layer 2 equal-cost multipath and are used for a variety of reasons. The MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute tools were not designed to discover and exercise specific paths of Layer 2 equal-cost multipath, which produces a limitation in the following scenario, where a label-switched path traverses a LAG:

  • Label switching over some member links of the LAG is successful but fails over other member links.
  • The MPLS echo request for the path over the LAG is load-balanced onto one of the member links that is label switching successfully.

In that situation MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute cannot detect the label-switching failure of the problematic member link. The lack of Layer 2 equal-cost multipath diagnostic coverage means the tools can be blind to label-switching failures over a problematic LAG interface, so it is desirable to extend them to give deterministic diagnostic coverage of LAG interfaces. The work towards a solution was motivated by issues encountered in live networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle of links behaves like one link, so a test packet is sent down whichever member the load balancer picks. If one member has stopped forwarding labels, the test may always land on a good member and the fault never shows up.

sections.title: How the Solution Fits Together
sections.content:
The document defines a new TLV for discovering the capabilities of a responder router, and extensions that let MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute describe multipath information for individual LAG member links. The reader is expected to be familiar with the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV of Section 3.4 of RFC 8029.

The solution is an MPLS echo request carrying a DDMAP TLV and the new LSR Capability TLV, to say that separate load-balancing information for each Layer 2 next hop over a LAG is wanted in the echo reply. The responder puts the same LSR Capability TLV in the echo reply as an acknowledgement, and adds, for each downstream LAG member, the load-balancing information, that is the multipath information and the interface index. The mechanism applies to all types of label-switched path that can traverse LAG interfaces.

Many LAGs are built from peer-to-peer links, where two routers have direct connectivity and the same number of LAG members. It is possible to build LAGs asymmetrically by putting Ethernet switches between the two routers. Appendix A lists use cases where the mechanisms may not apply. The mechanisms impose no changes on scenarios where a path is pinned to a particular LAG member, that is, where the LAG is not treated as one logical interface by the path.

In the example network, with A connected to B, B connected to C over a two-member LAG and to D over a plain link, and D and C connected to E, a traceroute from A to E makes node B return load-balancing information for four entries: the downstream C over the non-LAG upper path, the first downstream C over the LAG, the second downstream C over the LAG, and the downstream D over the non-LAG lower path.

The document then defines, in turn, a mechanism to discover the capabilities of responder routers, a mechanism to discover Layer 2 equal-cost multipath information, a mechanism to validate Layer 2 equal-cost multipath traversal, the LSR Capability TLV, the LAG Description Indicator flag, the Local Interface Index Sub-TLV, the Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV, and the Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The tester first asks what the far router can do, then asks for a list of the member links in each bundle, then sends test packets down each member in turn so that every one of them is checked.

sections.title: Discovering What a Router Supports
sections.content:
MPLS Ping works by an initiator router sending an MPLS echo request and receiving an echo reply from a responder router. MPLS Traceroute works in a similar way, except the initiator may send several echo requests with increasing TTL values.

Many extensions to these mechanisms have been made over the years, so it is often useful, and sometimes necessary, for the initiator to tell apart three cases: the responder sent the reply with certain contents because it has those features implemented, the responder sent it because it has only a subset of them implemented, and the responder sent it because it has none of them implemented.

The LSR Capability TLV makes that distinction possible. When the initiator wants to discover the capabilities of the responder, it includes the LSR Capability TLV in the echo request. When the responder receives an echo request carrying that TLV, then if it knows the TLV it MUST include it in the echo reply, describing the features and extensions the local router supports. If it does not know the TLV, it must send an echo reply with the return code set to "One or more of the TLVs was not understood", according to the rules in Section 3 of RFC 8029, and the initiator can then send another echo request without the TLV.

It is RECOMMENDED that implementations supporting the LAG multipath extensions include the LSR Capability TLV in echo requests. A responder that understands the TLV MUST include it in the reply, and if it understands the LAG Description Indicator flag it sets the Downstream LAG Info Accommodation flag when it can describe the outgoing LAG member links separately and clears it otherwise, and does the same with the Upstream LAG Info Accommodation flag for the incoming member links.
sections.plainLanguage: There have been so many extensions to ping and traceroute that an unfamiliar reply is ambiguous: the far router may not support the feature, may support part of it, or may support it fully. A small extra field in the request asks the far router to say which.

sections.title: Discovering the Member Links of a Bundle
sections.content:
Once the initiator knows the responder can describe incoming and outgoing LAG member links separately in the DDMAP TLV, it sends an MPLS echo request carrying a DDMAP TLV with the LAG Description Indicator flag, the G flag, set.

When a responder receives an echo request with the G flag set in the DDMAP TLV, and understands the flag and is able to describe outgoing LAG member links separately, it does the following for each downstream interface that is a LAG interface, whether or not the outgoing interfaces include LAG interfaces. It MUST include a DDMAP TLV in the echo reply, with a single DDMAP TLV for the LAG interface and the member links described using sub-TLVs. It MUST set the G flag in the DS Flags field. In the DDMAP TLV the Local Interface Index Sub-TLV, the Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV and the Multipath Data Sub-TLV describe each member link, while all the other fields describe the LAG interface.

For each member link the responder MUST add a Local Interface Index Sub-TLV with the LAG Member Link Indicator flag set, describing the interface index of that outgoing member link, which the local router assigns. It MAY add a Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV with the same flag set, describing the interface index of the incoming member link on the downstream router, which that downstream router assigns; how the local router obtains that index is outside the scope of this document. It MUST add a Multipath Data Sub-TLV for that member link if the received DDMAP TLV asked for multipath information.

The order of the sub-TLVs matters. The Local Interface Index Sub-TLV MUST be immediately followed by the Multipath Data Sub-TLV, except that a member link MAY also have a Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV, in which case the three are placed in the order Local Interface Index, Remote Interface Index and Multipath Data. The blocks for each member link MUST be adjacent to each other and in order of increasing local interface index. Where none of the received multipath information maps to a particular member link, the responder MUST still place the Local Interface Index Sub-TLV and the Multipath Data Sub-TLV for it, with the Multipath Length field set to zero.

The initiator then uses the reply to identify whether the responder can describe outgoing member links separately, to tell from the G flag whether each received DDMAP TLV describes a LAG interface or a plain one, and to obtain the multipath information expected to travel over the specific member link. When the initiator receives a DDMAP with LAG member information from a router with TTL=n, the DDMAP it sends onwards with TTL=n+1 through a particular member link must be updated: the Local Interface Index Sub-TLVs must be removed, the Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV for the member link being traversed should be kept if they were present and all the others removed, and the Multipath Data Sub-TLVs updated to include just one, either the one for the member link being traversed or a combination of them all.
sections.plainLanguage: The router at the far end lists each member link of the bundle, giving each an index, and says which label choices travel over it. The tester then reuses that list to steer the next probe down one chosen member.

sections.title: Checking That Each Member Link Is Used
sections.content:
The Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV describing the incoming member links of the downstream router is optional, because that information is often not available on the responder. Where it is missing, the traversal of the member links is validated by the procedures in Section 5.1. Where the routers can supply the Remote Interface Index Sub-TLVs, the validation in Section 5.2 can be used instead.

Without the downstream router returning Remote Interface Index Sub-TLVs, validation requires that the initiator traverses all the available member links and applies additional logic. The initiator sends an echo request carrying a DDMAP TLV with the Interface and Label Stack Object Request flag and the LAG Description Indicator flag set, to ask for the Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV with extra member link information. A responder that understands the flag and can describe the incoming member link should then add the Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV to the reply, and, if the incoming interface is a LAG, add the Incoming Interface Index Sub-TLV with the LAG Member Link Indicator flag set and the interface index of the member link that received the request.

With that, the initiator knows the expected load-balancing information of every member link at the router with TTL=n, the expected interface index of the outgoing member link at TTL=n for a given entropy, and the interface index of the incoming member link at TTL=n+1 for the same entropy. The expectation is that the messages that load-balance to outgoing member link X at TTL=n all reach the next hop on the same incoming member link Y at TTL=n+1.

The initiator sends two echo requests to traverse the two member links at TTL=n+1. In the success case one request reaches TTL=n+1 on member link 1 and the other on member link 2, so the two requests reach the immediate downstream router from two different member links. In the error case one request reaches TTL=n+1 on member link 1 and the other also reaches it on member link 1, or one or both of the requests cannot reach the immediate downstream router on whichever link.

These procedures give a deterministic result for LAG interfaces that are back-to-back connected between routers, with no Layer 2 switch in between. Where there is a Layer 2 switch between the router at TTL=n and the router at TTL=n+1, there is no guarantee that every incoming interface at TTL=n+1 can be traversed, even when every outgoing member link at TTL=n is traversed. Operator provisioning models should be considered when reading the output of a traceroute that exercises Layer 2 equal-cost multipath.

When the Remote Interface Index Sub-TLVs are available, the downstream router can do the validation instead, and the comparison of the incoming member link with the interface index in the sub-TLV is added to its own checks. A failure of that comparison results in the return code being set to "Downstream Mapping Mismatch (5)".
sections.plainLanguage: To confirm that every member link really is being used, the tester sends one probe per member and checks that the probes arrive at the far router on different members. If two probes arrive on the same member, that member is broken. The test is only conclusive when the two routers are directly connected.

sections.title: The New TLVs and Flags
sections.content:
The LSR Capability TLV MAY be included in the echo request and the echo reply, and neither message MUST include more than one of them. Its presence in a request asks the responder to include one in the reply. Its type is 4 and its length is 4. The LSR Capability Flags field is 4 octets long and holds two flags defined here, with the unallocated flags set to zero on sending and ignored on receipt. Both the U and D flags MUST be cleared in an echo request and ignored there, while zero, one or both MAY be set in an echo reply. The U flag, Upstream LAG Info Accommodation, is set when the router can describe a LAG member link in the Incoming Interface Index Sub-TLV. The D flag, Downstream LAG Info Accommodation, is set when it can describe LAG member links in the Local Interface Index Sub-TLV and the Multipath Data Sub-TLV.

The LAG Description Indicator flag, the G flag, is a new flag in the DS Flags field of the DDMAP TLV, at bit number 3. In an echo request it asks the responder for detailed LAG information. In an echo reply it MUST be set if the DDMAP TLV describes a LAG interface, and cleared otherwise.

The Local Interface Index Sub-TLV describes the interface index assigned by the local router to an egress interface, and one or more may appear in a DDMAP TLV. Its type is 4 and its length is 4, and the Local Interface Index field is 4 octets long, normally an unsigned integer in network byte order.

The Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV is optional and describes the interface index assigned by a downstream router to an ingress interface, and one or more may appear in a DDMAP TLV. Its type is 5 and its length is 4, and the index field is 4 octets long.

The Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV MAY be included in an echo reply to report the interface on which the request was received and the label stack that was on the packet when it arrived. A responder MUST NOT insert more than one of them. Its type is 6 and its length is the sum of the fields before the sub-TLVs plus the sub-TLV lengths. Its format is derived from the Interface and Label Stack TLV of RFC 8029, with the label stack turned into a sub-TLV and a new sub-TLV added to describe an interface index.

The Address Type says whether the interface is numbered or unnumbered and sets the length of the address and interface fields: type 1 is IPv4 Numbered at 16 octets, type 2 is IPv4 Unnumbered at 16 octets, type 3 is IPv6 Numbered at 40 octets and type 4 is IPv6 Unnumbered at 28 octets. IPv4 addresses and interface indices are encoded in 4 octets and IPv6 addresses in 16. For a numbered interface the address type must be the numbered one, the IP address is either the router's Router ID or the interface address, and the interface is the interface address. For an unnumbered interface the IP address is the router's Router ID and the interface is the index assigned to it.

Two sub-TLVs are defined for it. The Incoming Label Stack Sub-TLV, type 1, holds the label stack as received, with any TTL values changed by the router restored. The Incoming Interface Index Sub-TLV, type 2, has length 8 and describes the index the local router assigned to the interface that received the request. Its Interface Index Flags field is a bit vector with one flag defined, M, the LAG Member Link Indicator, set when the index describes a member of a LAG; the remaining flags must be zero on sending and ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new pieces of information are added to the ping reply: what the far router can do, the index of each member link of a bundle, and which member link actually received the probe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document extends the LSP Traceroute mechanism of RFC 8029 to discover and exercise Layer 2 equal-cost multipath paths and to determine which member link of a LAG is problematic. These on-demand diagnostic mechanisms are used by an operator inside an MPLS control domain, and RFC 8029 reviews the possible attacks and the approaches to mitigate them.

To prevent leaking information to untrusted users, a responder router MUST only accept MPLS echo requests from designated trusted sources, by filtering the source IP address field of the received requests. As RFC 8029 notes, spoofing attacks have only a small window of opportunity. If an intermediate node hijacks these messages, that is, causes them not to be delivered, using these mechanisms will show that the data plane is not working as it should. Hijacking a responder node so that it gives a legitimate reply would mean compromising the node itself and the MPLS control domain, and RFC 5920 gives additional network-wide recommendations for avoiding such attacks. The document notes that source address filtering is only a weak form of access control and is not a reliable security mechanism in general, but it is required here in the absence of anything more robust.
sections.plainLanguage: These probes reveal information about the network, so a router should only answer them from trusted sources. Address filtering is a weak control, but it is better than nothing and it is what the document requires.

viz.caption: WHY THE OLD TOOLS CANNOT SEE THE FAULT (RFC 8611, SECTION 1.1)

items.title: The bundle behaves as one link
items.text: The layer switched path crosses a Link Aggregation Group, which the ping tools treat as a single interface.

items.title: Some members work, some do not
items.text: Label switching succeeds over some member links of the group and fails over others.

items.title: The probe is balanced at random
items.text: The echo request is load-balanced onto one of the member links, and it may be one that works.

items.title: So the fault stays invisible
items.text: Without layer 2 diagnostic coverage, the tools cannot detect the label-switching failure on the bad member link.

messages.label: Echo reply with four paths
messages.note: Downstream C over the plain link, C over each of the two LAG members, and D over the plain link.

viz.caption: THE NEW CODES AND FLAGS (RFC 8611, SECTIONS 6 TO 10 AND 13)

items.label: LSR Capability TLV
items.desc: Type 4, length 4. Asks the responder what it supports.

items.label: Local Interface Index Sub-TLV
items.desc: Type 4, length 4. The index the local router gave an egress interface.

items.label: Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV
items.desc: Type 5, length 4. The index the downstream router gave an ingress interface.

items.label: Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV
items.desc: Type 6. Reports the receiving interface and the incoming label stack.

items.label: G, LAG Description Indicator
items.desc: In the DS Flags field. Asks for detailed LAG information, and marks a reply that carries it.

items.label: U and D capability flags
items.desc: Set in the reply when the router can describe incoming or outgoing member links separately.

items.label: M, LAG Member Link Indicator
items.desc: In the Interface Index Flags field. Marks an index that names a member of a bundle.

cells: One probe reaches the next hop on member link 1 and the other on member link 2.
Both probes reach the next hop on member link 1, or one or both fail to reach the next hop.
